periods.activity_title: First Meeting with Badal and Moti

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the story by asking children what they know about puppies and village life, drawing on their own experiences to prepare them for the characters they are about to meet.

The teacher reads the prose text on pp.15–17 aloud with expression, pausing at the moment Badal finds the shivering puppy and again at the pit scene to let the drama land. Children follow in their textbooks.
The teacher reads the text a second time, this time inviting children to join in on repeated phrases and the naming of Moti, building familiarity with the story language.
Children close their books and the teacher asks one or two plain recall questions — who is Badal? what did he find? — as an unhurried oral check.

periods.teacher_notes: The story's emotional arc — shivering puppy found, friendship built, rescue earned — is most powerful when children first hear it uninterrupted. Resist the urge to explain every word during the first read.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — A (pp.18): answer questions 1–4 on Badal finding the puppy, naming Moti, the pit, and Moti's rescue.

time_bands.activity: Children re-read pp.15–17 silently, then the teacher briefly re-reads the pit-and-rescue passage aloud so the crisis sequence is fresh in every child's mind before discussion.

The class works through questions 1–4 from Let us think — A (p.18) together: the teacher asks each question, waits for hands, invites answers, and helps children locate evidence in the text — what Badal found, what they named the puppy, what Badal fell into, how Moti tracked him.
Children write their answers to questions 1–4 in their notebooks; the teacher circulates and gives brief spoken feedback on sentence completeness.
The teacher brings the class back together and confirms the four answers orally, correcting any recurring errors in phrasing.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often confuse 'scent' with 'sight' when explaining how Moti found Badal — question 4 is the key diagnostic. Encourage them to use the word 'scent' or 'smell' in their answer, drawing directly from the story language on pp.15–17.

periods.activity_title: True or False — Reading for Accuracy

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — A (p.18): true/false items (a)–(e) on Badal's household, Moti's loyalty, and the rescue sequence.

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly recaps the story's key facts — Badal lives with his mother, Moti grows into his best friend, the pit rescue — as a spoken warm-up before the accuracy task.

The class works through the five true/false statements (Let us think — A, p.18) one by one: teacher reads each statement aloud, children decide, then the class discusses what the correct answer is and why, pointing back to the text on pp.15–17.

Children write T or F for each statement in their notebooks with a brief reason in their own words; the teacher circulates and prompts children who write 'T' for the grandmother and photo statements to re-read the relevant lines.
Teacher reads the five statements once more and the class calls out T or F together, ending with a quick whole-class confirmation of the correct sequence of events.

periods.teacher_notes: Two statements are designed as traps: that Badal lived with his grandmother (he lived with his mother) and that Moti caught Badal's photo (he caught his scent). These test careful reading rather than general memory and reward children who can point to specific lines.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — B (p.19): pair discussion on falling down, pets they know, and the animal they would choose as a pet.

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with a playful question to the class — 'Has anyone here ever slipped and fallen somewhere surprising?' — taking two or three quick responses to warm the room before structured pair talk begins.

Children work in pairs on Let us think — B (p.19): they share the story of their last fall, then talk about pets they have or know, taking turns to listen and respond. The teacher circulates, prompting shy children with 'Who picked you up?' or 'What does the pet do?'

Pairs now discuss the third prompt — which animal would you keep as a pet and why? The teacher listens in to two or three pairs and then invites one child from each to share their choice with the class, giving a reason in a full sentence.
Brief whole-class round-up: teacher notes the range of animals chosen on the board and asks children whether Moti — a dog — would be a good choice, connecting the discussion back to the story.

periods.teacher_notes: Children at this stage benefit from knowing exactly when to listen and when to speak in a pair. A brief modelled exchange at the start ('I fell when I was running to the gate; my father picked me up') gives reluctant speakers a sentence shape to borrow.

periods.activity_title: Listen and Sequence — The Story in Order

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen — A (p.20): listen to the story read aloud, then number the six story events in the correct sequence.

time_bands.activity: The teacher explains the task: children will listen to the story of Badal and Moti read aloud and then put six printed events in the order they happened. Books are placed face-down on desks.
The teacher reads the story transcript aloud slowly and clearly, a total of three times with brief pauses between each reading, so children can hold the sequence in their minds.

Children open their textbooks to p.20 and write the numbers 1–6 next to the events on Let us listen — A; the first event (Badal came across a puppy) is already marked, so children sequence the remaining five.
The teacher reads each event aloud in story order and asks children to call out the number they wrote; the class builds the correct sequence together on the board or by show of hands.
Teacher asks one child to retell the story in three sentences using only the correctly ordered events as prompts — a quick oral close to the listening task.

periods.teacher_notes: The sequencing task is harder than it looks because two events — Moti accompanying the search and Moti following the scent — are close together and easy to swap. After confirming the correct order, ask children what happens between those two events to help them see the causal link.

periods.activity_title: My Daily Routine — Talking About Every Day

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak — A (p.21): pair talk about daily routine — before school, during school, after school.
Let us speak — B (p.21): use the sentence-frame clues to describe the full daily routine aloud in pairs.

time_bands.activity: The teacher models one sentence about her own morning routine — 'Every day I wake up at six in the morning, then I brush my teeth' — to show how the sentence frame on p.21 works before children try it themselves.

Pairs take turns answering Let us speak — A (p.21): one child describes what she does before school, her partner listens and then shares what she does during school hours, then they swap roles for the 'after school' prompt.

Children now use the sentence-frame clues in Let us speak — B (p.21) to build a fuller description of their morning routine; they fill in the blanks mentally or in a whisper and then say the whole paragraph aloud to their partner.
Three or four children share their routine with the class in full sentences; the teacher gives quick encouraging feedback on sentence completeness and correct use of time words.

periods.teacher_notes: The sentence frames in Let us speak — B carry children who are uncertain where to start, but push confident speakers to add one detail the frame does not supply. Nudge the stronger speakers to go beyond the printed scaffold while keeping the frame available for all.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — A (p.19): add -ed to walk, play, talk, ask, touch; notice that -ed marks past action from the story words.

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes the story words lived, loved, played, gathered, thanked on the board and asks children what all five have in common. Once they notice -ed, the teacher explains: these are things that already happened in Badal and Moti's story.

Working through Let us learn — A (p.19), the teacher models the first one — walk + ed = walked — then children complete play, talk, ask, touch on their own in their notebooks; the teacher circulates and checks for double-letters or dropped endings.

The teacher writes the five base words on the board and invites children one by one to come up and write the -ed form, then use the new word in a spoken sentence about something Badal or Moti did in the story.
Quick oral drill: teacher calls a base word, children call the -ed form in chorus — a brisk, unhurried chant to consolidate the pattern before moving on.

periods.teacher_notes: Children sometimes add -eed or -d instead of -ed for words already ending in e (played → plaid is a common error). Reinforce that these five words simply take -ed with no change to the base, using the story examples as the reference point.

periods.activity_title: Word Pairs — Things That Go Together

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — B (p.20): match the six word pairs (bat–ball, needle–thread, paper–pencil, chair–table, lock–key, idli–sambar) and colour each pair.

time_bands.activity: The teacher says 'bat and…' and waits — children call out 'ball!'. The teacher does this with two more well-known pairs to establish the idea that some words belong together before opening the textbook.

Children work on Let us learn — B (p.20), drawing lines to match the six word pairs and colouring each matched pair in the same colour; two pairs are already done as examples, so children complete the remaining four.

The teacher reviews the pairs whole-class by calling out one word and inviting different children to supply the partner; for idli–sambar the teacher connects this to familiar food to celebrate the cultural reference.
Extension oral game: teacher invites children to suggest new word pairs from their own lives — shoe and…, pencil and… — practising the pattern in a playful, open-ended way.

periods.teacher_notes: The pair idli–sambar is a culturally specific combination that may be unfamiliar to some children; welcome children who suggest a locally known food pair instead, validating their world while keeping the grammatical pattern clear.

periods.activity_title: Ordering a Picture Story — The Pigeon and the Ant

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write — A (p.21): study the six jumbled pictures of the pigeon and ant story and number them in the correct story order.

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly narrates the pigeon-and-ant story orally without naming the order: 'A dove rested by a stream. An ant fell in. The dove helped. A hunter appeared. The ant saved the dove.' Children listen before looking at the pictures.

Children study the six jumbled pictures on p.21 in Let us write — A; working individually, they decide the story order and write numbers 1–6 in the boxes provided. The teacher circulates and asks children to explain a choice aloud when uncertain.
The class shares their numbering; the teacher draws six blank boxes on the board and fills in the agreed sequence as children call it out, briefly discussing any disagreements.
One child retells the whole story sequence in spoken sentences using only the picture order as a guide — connecting the visual task to oral storytelling.

periods.teacher_notes: The pictures for this task are in the textbook on p.21; children need to look carefully at the cause-and-effect logic (ant saved by leaf, then ant saves dove) to get the hunter picture in the right place. The spoken narration at the end confirms whether the ordering was understood or guessed.

periods.activity_title: Fill the Story — Words That Complete the Tale

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write — B (p.22): fill all six blanks in the pigeon-and-ant passage using the box words: leaf, flew, branch, climbed, fell, stream, hunter.

homework.task_brief: Let us write — C (p.22): add a full stop or question mark to each of the six sentences at home and be ready to explain the choice.

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the incomplete passage on p.22 aloud, pausing dramatically at each blank to let children hear where the story needs a word; this oral preview primes them for the fill-in work.
Teacher and class quickly name and clarify the seven box words — leaf, flew, branch, climbed, fell, stream, hunter — with a quick mime or gesture for any that are unfamiliar.

Children work through Let us write — B (p.22) independently, writing one word in each blank; the teacher circulates and gives spoken hints to children who are stuck — 'The ant went into the water — what's another word for a small river?'
The teacher reads the full passage with the correct words inserted; children check their own work and correct any errors in a different colour.

The teacher explains tonight's homework — Let us write — C (p.22), adding a full stop or question mark to each of the six sentences — and reads two examples with the class so they understand the choice.

periods.teacher_notes: The word 'fell' appears both as a past action (the ant fell) and could be confused with 'flew' for the dove's exit. Encourage children to re-read the whole sentence before choosing, rather than picking the first plausible word from the box.

periods.activity_title: Adding to the Picture — Children Playing Together

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us do — A (p.24): study the picture of three children playing outdoors and add new elements using crayons or colour pencils.

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks children to look at the illustration on p.24 quietly for a moment and say aloud one thing they notice — the hoop, the ball, the swing — before picking up their crayons, building shared attention to the scene.

Teacher invites a quick brainstorm: 'What else might children be playing? What else might be in this outdoor space — a tree, a dog, a kite?' A few suggestions are called out and the teacher notes them on the board as inspiration, not instruction.

Children work on Let us do — A (p.24), adding their own elements to the picture using crayons or colour pencils; the teacher circulates, asks each child one question about what they have added and why, encouraging a spoken sentence.
Four or five children hold up their textbooks and describe what they added in one or two sentences; the class listens and notices similarities and differences across pictures.
The teacher connects the theme of playing together back to the friendship between Badal and Moti, closing the activity with a brief spoken reflection on what makes a good friend or companion.

periods.teacher_notes: The illustration in the textbook on p.24 already contains three children with a hoop, a ball, and a swing; the space is intentionally open so children can add whatever speaks to their play experience. Welcome additions that reflect local games or outdoor settings the children know.

periods.activity_title: Bringing It All Together — Badal, Moti, and Us

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites children to recall the full arc of the Badal and Moti story — puppy found, friendship grown, crisis in the pit, rescue by scent — as a spoken summary; two or three children contribute sentences to build a shared retelling.

Quick word-work revisit: the teacher writes three base words on the board — thank, play, gather — and asks children to change them to past tense with -ed, then use each in a spoken sentence about the story, connecting grammar to meaning.

Children write three sentences of their own in their notebooks: one describing Badal's character, one describing Moti's loyalty, and one explaining what the story teaches about friendship — a short independent response that draws the story themes together.

Children share their friendship sentences with a partner, listen to each other's ideas, and together decide which sentence they like best and why — a brief paired oracy exchange rooted in what they have written.

The teacher leads an observational curiosity moment: 'Think of any animal — a dog, a cat, a bird — that you have seen helping or comforting someone. What did it do?' Two or three children share a brief observation, connecting the story's theme to the real world.
The teacher closes by reading the story's final moment — Badal hugging and thanking Moti — aloud from p.17, letting the words carry the chapter to a quiet close.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws on the prose story, the -ed past-tense pattern, and the themes of friendship and loyalty that the chapter explores. Children's written sentences and spoken retelling are the evidence of learning; there is no prior draft or artefact this unit depends on.

items.source_lo: Student answers literal and inferential comprehension questions using a prose story as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Badal finds a shivering puppy, names it Moti; Moti rescues Badal from a pit by following his scent.
items.item_stem: How did Moti know where to find Badal when he fell into the pit?

options.label: A
options.text: A neighbour tied a rope to Moti and led him to the pit.

options.label: B
options.text: Badal's mother showed Moti a photograph of the lane.

options.label: C
options.text: Moti followed Badal's scent and barked near the pit.

options.label: D
options.text: Moti saw Badal fall from a distance and ran to the spot.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests the student confused scent-tracking with sight, picturing Moti as a witness rather than a tracker.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Reveals a confusion with the false true/false statement in the story exercises about Moti catching Badal's photo.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Indicates the student has merged Moti's role with the neighbours' rope-and-rescue action, not distinguishing who did what.

items.source_context: Badal finds a shivering puppy, names it Moti; Moti rescues Badal from a pit by following his scent.
items.item_stem: Badal's mother said he could keep the puppy only on one condition. What was that condition, and do you think Badal kept his promise? Give one reason from the story.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Badal's mother said he could keep the puppy only if he promised to take care of it. The story shows he kept his promise because Moti grew up to be his devoted best friend, which means Badal cared for him well.

items.item_stem: Your teacher will read the story of Badal and Moti aloud. Listen carefully. Then read these three events and choose which one happened FIRST in the story.

options.label: A
options.text: Badal and his mother named the puppy Moti.

options.label: B
options.text: Badal came across a shivering puppy by the side of the road.

options.label: C
options.text: Badal slipped on a muddy lane and fell into a deep pit.

options.label: D
options.text: Moti followed Badal's scent and went near the pit.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests the student remembered the rescue scene most vividly and placed it first, without tracking the story's opening.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Indicates the student identified an early event but missed that finding the puppy precedes the naming scene.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals a focus on the crisis event without recognising the earlier stages of the story.

items.item_stem: After listening to the story of Badal and Moti, retell what happened from the moment Badal's mother gathered the neighbours to the moment Badal hugged Moti. Use at least three events in the correct order.

expected_elements: Mentions the mother gathering neighbours to search.
Describes Moti following scent and barking at the pit.
Names the neighbours pulling Badal out and Badal hugging Moti.

items.item_stem: Which of the following is something a child would do BEFORE coming to school?

options.label: C
options.text: Go to sleep for the night.

options.label: D
options.text: Play with friends in the evening.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests the child has not connected 'before school' to morning time; confusion between evening and morning routines.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Indicates the child is thinking of after-school time rather than the morning before school.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Reveals a conflation of after-school activities with the morning routine.
